howToEdit: Every term the app can define. Edit the wording freely: it changes words, never numbers. 'aliases' are the exact words that link to the entry in Expert Mode — an alias with a capital letter matches case-sensitively (ROIC, Ke), an all-lowercase one matches any case (owner earnings). GlossaryTest fails if Expert Mode shows an abbreviation that no entry defines. Xcode and Gradle rebuild when this file changes.

entries.plain: What a business is actually worth per share, judged by the cash it earns — not by what people are paying for it today. Alpha estimates it two ways from the company's own SEC filings.
entries.expert: Present value of the cash an owner can take out of the business over its life. Model A uses Graham's earnings multiple and Buffett's owner earnings; Model B discounts projected free cash flow to the firm at WACC.

entries.plain: The discount between the price and what the business is worth. Buying at 25–50% below intrinsic value leaves room to be wrong. If the price is above the value, there is no margin — just risk.
entries.expert: MoS = 1 − price ÷ intrinsic value. Graham's central rule: the estimate is uncertain, so demand a price far enough below it that errors in the estimate don't lose money.

entries.plain: The cash a business could hand to its owners each year after paying to keep itself running. Buffett's preferred measure of what a company really makes.
entries.expert: Net income + depreciation & amortization − maintenance capital expenditure ± change in working capital. Alpha proxies maintenance capex as min(capex, D&A) and labels it.

entries.plain: Cash from operations minus what was spent on equipment and buildings. It's the money left over after the business invests in itself.
entries.expert: Cash from operating activities − capital expenditures (levered FCF). Model B uses FCFF — unlevered, after-tax operating cash flow before interest.

entries.plain: How much profit the company earns for every dollar invested in it. High and steady returns are the signature of a business with a durable advantage.
entries.expert: NOPAT ÷ invested capital (equity + debt − cash). Compared with WACC: a positive, persistent spread indicates an economic moat.

entries.plain: The return investors and lenders expect for putting money into this company. Future cash is discounted at this rate — the riskier the business, the higher it is and the less future cash is worth today.
entries.expert: Weighted average of cost of equity (CAPM: risk-free + β × equity risk premium) and after-tax cost of debt, weighted by market value of equity and debt.

entries.plain: How much the stock swings compared with the overall market. 1.0 moves with the market; 0.5 is calmer; 1.5 is wilder. Alpha measures it from five years of monthly prices — it is never just assumed.
entries.expert: Slope of the regression of the stock's monthly returns on the S&P 500's over 5 years (≥ 36 months required). R² shows how much of the movement the market explains.

entries.plain: What the accountants say the company owns minus what it owes. A floor of sorts — though for modern companies brands and software rarely show up in it.
entries.expert: Shareholders' equity from the balance sheet. Per share = equity ÷ diluted shares. NNWC (net-net working capital) is Graham's harsher liquidation view.

entries.plain: A quick rule from Benjamin Graham: a company's value is its earnings per share times a multiple that grows with expected growth. Adjusted for today's interest rates.
entries.expert: V* = EPS × (8.5 + 2g) × 4.4 ÷ Y, where g is expected growth (capped at 15%) and Y the current AAA corporate bond yield.

entries.plain: Before Alpha shows a value, it tests the numbers it pulled from SEC: do the books balance, are the figures recent, is anything assumed rather than measured? Failures block the value; warnings are shown beside it.
entries.expert: Balance-sheet identity, EPS vs NI/shares, share-count plausibility, TTM period alignment, filing and price freshness, sign sanity, and provenance of beta, tax rate, cost of debt and rates.

entries.plain: The company's profit for the year divided by its number of shares — the slice of profit that belongs to one share.
entries.expert: Diluted EPS = net income ÷ diluted weighted-average shares, as filed. The trailing-twelve-month figure is built additively (full year + year-to-date − prior year-to-date), so it is exact only when the share count is steady.

entries.plain: The most recent full year of results, ending at the latest quarterly report rather than the last fiscal year-end — the freshest year-long picture available.
entries.expert: Flows: the last 10-K fiscal year + the current year-to-date from the latest 10-Q − the same year-to-date a year earlier. Balance-sheet items: the latest filed balance sheet.

entries.plain: The yearly return shareholders expect for owning the stock, given how risky it is. A business has to earn more than this to create value for its owners.
entries.expert: CAPM: rf + β × ERP, floored at rf + 4% so a very low measured beta can't imply an implausibly cheap cost of equity. The metric says when the floor applied.

entries.plain: The interest rate the company pays on what it borrows.
entries.expert: Interest expense ÷ total debt from the filings, clamped to 2–12%. When interest isn't tagged, rf + 1.5% is assumed and flagged. It enters WACC after tax: Kd × (1 − t).

entries.plain: A standard formula for the return investors demand from a stock: the rate on a safe government bond, plus extra for how much the stock moves with the market.
entries.expert: Capital asset pricing model: Ke = rf + β × ERP, with rf the 10-year Treasury yield.

entries.plain: The extra yearly return investors demand for owning stocks instead of safe government bonds.
entries.expert: A policy assumption (5% by default), editable in Settings. Multiplied by beta in CAPM.

entries.plain: What a safe investment pays — here, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield. Every other required return is built on top of it.
entries.expert: FRED series DGS10, published daily to the app's rates file; editable in Settings.

entries.term: Free cash flow to the firm (FCFF)
aliases: free cash flow to the firm
entries.plain: The cash the business produces for everyone who funded it — shareholders and lenders — before any interest is paid.
entries.expert: NOPAT + D&A − capex − the normalized change in working capital. Model B projects it and discounts it at WACC; shareholders' value is what remains after subtracting debt and adding cash.

entries.plain: Valuing a business by estimating the cash it will produce in future years and converting that into what it is worth today.
entries.expert: Model B: FCFF grown at the stage-one rate over the projection years, plus a terminal value, each discounted at WACC. A business that consumes cash can't be valued this way, so no DCF value is shown for it.

entries.plain: What the business is assumed to be worth beyond the years projected in detail. It is often the largest part of a DCF value, which is why its assumptions matter.
entries.expert: Model B computes two — a perpetuity growing at the terminal rate (2.5% by default) and an exit multiple of the last year's cash flow (15× by default) — and averages the resulting values. Both assumptions are editable.

entries.plain: Operating profit after tax, as if the company had no debt — what the business itself earns before financing choices.
entries.expert: Operating income × (1 − effective tax rate).

entries.plain: Profit for every dollar of shareholders' own money in the business. The key measure for banks and insurers.
entries.expert: Net income ÷ shareholders' equity. Not shown when equity is negative (after heavy buybacks), where the ratio has no meaning.

entries.plain: The steady yearly growth rate that would take a figure from its starting value to its ending value, smoothing out the bumpy years in between.
entries.expert: (last ÷ first)^(1 ÷ years) − 1. Undefined when either end is zero or negative.

entries.plain: Benjamin Graham's liquidation test: roughly what shareholders would get if the company sold its short-term assets at a discount and paid off everything it owes.
entries.expert: Cash + short-term investments + 75% of receivables + 50% of inventory − total liabilities. Negative for most operating businesses; a positive figure per share above the price is Graham's 'net-net' bargain.

entries.plain: The cash tied up in running the business day to day — stock on shelves and bills customers haven't paid yet, less bills the company hasn't paid yet.
entries.expert: (Current assets − cash − short-term investments) − (current liabilities − short-term debt). Owner earnings and FCFF use a normalized yearly change: the 5-year average of NWC ÷ revenue × the change in revenue.

entries.plain: The yearly accounting charge for equipment and buildings wearing out (depreciation) and purchased intangibles being used up (amortization). It reduces profit, but no cash leaves the business that year.
entries.expert: Added back in owner earnings, FCFF and FFO. Maintenance capex is proxied as the smaller of capex and D&A.

entries.plain: Money spent on long-lived assets — factories, equipment, stores, software.
entries.expert: Payments for property, plant and equipment from the cash-flow statement. The part needed just to stay in place (maintenance capex) isn't disclosed, so Alpha uses the smaller of capex and D&A and labels it.

entries.plain: The REIT version of earnings: net income with property depreciation added back and one-off property-sale gains removed, because well-kept buildings don't wear out the way machines do.
entries.expert: NAREIT definition: net income + D&A − gains on sale of property. Model A applies Graham's formula to FFO per share.

entries.plain: The share price divided by book value per share — how many dollars investors pay for each dollar of net assets on the books.
entries.expert: For banks and insurers the justified multiple is P/B* = (ROE − g) ÷ (Ke − g), capped at 4×: worth more than book only when returns on equity beat the cost of equity.

entries.plain: The share price divided by earnings per share — how many years of today's profit you pay for.
entries.expert: Graham's 8.5 is the P/E he considered fair for a company with no growth.

entries.plain: Profit left over after charging the business for all the capital it uses. Positive means it earns more than its investors require.
entries.expert: (ROIC − WACC) × invested capital.

entries.plain: A way to value banks and insurers: book value today, plus the value of future profits above what shareholders require.
entries.expert: V = B0 + Σ (ROE − Ke) × prior book value ÷ (1 + Ke)^t + TV, where B0 is today's book value.

entries.plain: The interest rate paid by the safest corporate borrowers. Graham scaled his formula by it: when high-grade bonds pay more, stocks deserve lower prices.
entries.expert: Moody's seasoned Aaa corporate bond yield (FRED series DAAA). In the revised Graham formula it is Y, set against the 4.4% of Graham's day.

entries.plain: The cash dividend paid for each share over the year.
entries.expert: Used by the dividend discount model for REITs: V = DPS × (1 + g) ÷ (Ke − g).

entries.plain: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, which requires public companies to file audited reports. EDGAR is its public database — every figure in Alpha comes from it.
entries.expert: Figures come from the XBRL data in 10-K (annual) and 10-Q (quarterly) filings, through SEC's companyfacts feed or, when that lags, from the filing itself.

entries.plain: The SEC's permanent ID number for a company, used to find its filings on EDGAR.
entries.expert: Central Index Key. It survives ticker changes; a holding-company reorganization creates a new one, which is why ExxonMobil's history comes from its predecessor.

entries.plain: A four-digit industry code the SEC assigns each company. Alpha uses it to decide whether a company is valued as an operating business, a bank or insurer, or a REIT.
entries.expert: Standard Industrial Classification from the filer's SEC profile: 6798 is REITs; the 6020–6411 range covers banks, brokers and insurers.

entries.plain: The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis's free economic database — the source of the Treasury and AAA bond yields Alpha uses.
entries.expert: Series DGS10 and DAAA, published daily to the app's rates file on GitHub Pages; the app never holds an API key.

entries.plain: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles — the U.S. rules companies follow when preparing their financial statements.
entries.expert: XBRL tags in the us-gaap taxonomy tie each filed figure to one of these standard definitions.

entries.plain: Real estate investment trust — a company that owns property or mortgages and must pay out most of its income as dividends.
entries.expert: Property REITs are valued on FFO; mortgage REITs, which own loans rather than buildings, are valued like a bank, on book value and return on equity.

entries.plain: Profit from the business's own operations, before interest on its debt and before tax.
entries.expert: Earnings before interest and taxes. Taken from the filed operating income; when a company doesn't tag one (JNJ), Alpha uses pre-tax income + interest expense and labels it.

entries.plain: The company's own twelve-month accounting year. It doesn't have to match the calendar — Apple's ends in late September.
entries.expert: Labeled by the calendar year in which it mostly falls; 52/53-week years ending in the first days of January count toward the year before.

entries.plain: Results from the start of the company's fiscal year up to its latest quarterly report.
entries.expert: Quarterly reports (10-Q) give year-to-date totals; the trailing twelve months are built from them: last full year + this year-to-date − last year's year-to-date.

entries.plain: The trade association for U.S. real estate investment trusts. Its definition of funds from operations is the one the industry uses.
entries.expert: National Association of Real Estate Investment Trusts. Its FFO: net income + real-estate depreciation − gains on sale of property.

entries.plain: The minimum yearly return you want before an investment is worth making. Buffett's owner-earnings value discounts at it: the higher your bar, the less the business is worth to you.
entries.expert: A policy assumption (10% by default), editable in Settings. Owner earnings per share ÷ hurdle rate gives the no-growth value; Alpha also shows the same value at the 10-year Treasury yield for contrast.
